background.definition: Tinea versicolor (TV) or pityriasis versicolor is a superficial infection of the stratum corneum caused by a dimorphic, lipophilic yeast from the genus Malassezia, particularly Malassezia furfur. Skin lesions appear as hypopigmented, hyperpigmented or red-tan macules and patches associated with fine scaling. TV is usually asymptomatic, but may be associated with mild pruritus, and affects the chest, back, upper arms, neck and, sometimes, the face.

list.listitem: Most common among 21-30 age group, when sebaceous glands are most active.
Highest incidence is seen in tropical climates where it may present not only in adults, but also in children of all age groups.
Although rare, TV has also been reported in the elderly over 60 years of age.
TV accounts for 110 office visits per 100,000 persons per year to medical practitioners (eg, family physicians, pediatricians, dermatologists).
Malassezia globosa (90%) in its mycelial form is the predominant species of Malassezia furfur found in TV lesions. Malassezia sympodialis is less commonly seen.
Another name for this yeast is Pityrosporum (ovale and orbiculare).
TV is caused by Malassezia furfur, a saprophytic yeast that normally colonizes the stratum corneum.

In the presence of risk factors, the fungus is converted to its mycelial form and invades the dermis. It inhibits pigment transfer to keratinocytes by producing azelaic acid. This gives the lesions their classical hypopigmented appearance.
Exposure to sunlight accentuates the lesions because they do not tan like the surrounding normal skin.
Color changes other than hypopigmentation are possibly due to skin inflammation produced by the yeast.

Prophylactic treatment with oral itraconazole (200 mg twice daily one day per month) is safe and appears better than placebo (NNT = 3) in preventing recurrence of tinea versicolor in patients who have cleared the infection with oral itraconazole. B
Oral ketoconazole has not been studied in prospective RCTs for prophylaxis but is probably effective. C

Confirm the diagnosis by looking for "spaghetti and meatball" pattern of Malassezia on KOH exam of skin scrapings. C
Pale yellow to white fluorescence on Wood's lamp examination is seen in 62% of cases in children, 38% in older patients. C

Differential.Differential_Features: Hyperpigmented or erythematous, hyperkeratotic, verrucous, confluent papules or reticulated plaques with scale distributed along the upper back, chest and neck; negative KOH exam.
Erythematous patches and plaques with greasy scale, often associated with hypopigmentation in skin of color.
Hypopigmented macules and patches of the face and, less frequently, the upper extremities, with occasional fine scale.
Discrete, scalloped, depigmented patches without scale and negative KOH exam.
Erythematous, salmon-colored, elliptical patches and plaques with fine collarette of scale in a characteristic "Christmas tree" pattern on the trunk, preceded by a "herald patch"; negative KOH exam.
Discrete erythematous or hyperpigmented patches in the axillae or groin, with coral-red fluorescence on Wood's lamp exam.
Pruritic, expanding, erythematous, annular plaques with scale and central clearing, affecting the trunk and extremities.
Nonscaly, pale red to pink or pigmented discrete round macules distributed on the trunk, proximal extremities and soles.
Persistent localized or generalized patches, plaques or erythroderma of the trunk and extremities; often hard to diagnose (without a biopsy) and mistaken for eczema or psoriasis.
Hypopigmented macules or plaques associated with diminished sensation.
Solitary or multiple asymptomatic ovoid, hypopigmented "ash-leaf" macules on the trunk and limbs without scale. Wood's lamp makes lesions prominent.

list.listitem: Hypopigmented, hyperpigmented, or salmon-colored macules and patches with well-defined border and fine scale provide good evidence in favor of TV. Lesions are mostly asymptomatic or mildly pruritic.
Patients most often complain of cosmetically-disturbing dyspigmentation. TV may be hyperpigmented in dark-skinned individuals.
TV is more common in the tropical and subtropical areas, where the climate is hot and humid. It is also more common during the summer months.

Obtain a sample from the scaling patches using the side of a microscopic slide, scalpel blade in adults, or clear vinyl tape in children. Powdery scale not obvious on inspection can be demonstrated by scraping lightly with #15 scalpel blade or the side of a microscope slide.

Diagnosis is made by microscopic examination of skin scrapings after adding 10%-20% potassium hydroxide (KOH). Adding methylene blue or the blue or black ink enhances visualization of hyphae. Swartz-Lamkins fungal stain combines blue ink, KOH, and dimethyl sulfoxide (DMSO) for easy preparation and visualization. Adult patients demonstrate hyphae and yeast cells, whereas children most often demonstrate only hyphae.

Wood's lamp exam is a simple and easy technique reported in some studies to confirm diagnosis of TV in up to 62% of the patients. TV lesions have a pale yellow to white florescence. The test is less sensitive in older patients (38% in one study).
Culture of the skin scrapings using Sabouraud dextrose or modified Dixon agar is infrequently needed for diagnosis.
Histopathology of skin lesions shows hyphae and budding yeast when stained with periodic acid schiff (PAS) or methenamine silver stain.
See for the suggested approach to diagnosis and treatment of TV.

Treat uncomplicated tinea versicolor (TV) with topical antifungals like the azoles (ketoconazole, clotrimazole, econazole, and miconazole), allylamines (terbinafine), and other agents (ciclopirox, selenium sulfide) is effective. A
For extensive tinea versicolor or disease refractory to topical therapies, consider azole oral antifungals like fluconazole, ketoconazole, and itraconazole. B

See for an overview of topical and oral antifungal drug dosing for TV. A systematic review of 93 controlled trials with over 8327 patients concluded that most studies were of poor quality and that there was no good evidence to favor one intervention over another. In general, longer treatments and with higher concentrations (topical) were more effective.

Topical therapy is the mainstay of treatment and is preferred when lesions are localized. Commonly used topical antifungals are the imidazoles (ketoconazole, fluconazole), allylamines (terbinafine), and other agents like selenium sulfide and ciclopirox.
Oral antifungals are convenient and preferable for patients with widespread lesions. Effective drugs include azole antifungals like fluconazole, itraconazole, and ketoconazole.

Single dose 400 mg of oral fluconazole provides the best clinical and mycological cure rate compared to ketoconazole 400 mg single dose, ketoconazole 200 mg daily for 10 days, fluconazole 150 mg per week for 4 weeks, or single dose 400 mg of oral itraconazole.

A single dose of 300 mg of fluconazole repeated weekly for 2 weeks or a single dose of 400 mg of oral fluconazole or a single dose 400 mg of ketoconazole repeated weekly for 2 weeks are equally effective treatments for TV.
A single 400 mg dose of itraconazole has been found to be as effective as the 7-day 200 mg of daily dose of itraconazole in two small randomized trials.

Ketoconazole 2% shampoo used either as a single application or daily for 3 days is safe and effective in the treatment of TV. The shampoo was applied onto the dampened skin of all affected areas with lathering and left in place for 5 minutes. Clinical response rates at one month were 73%, 69%, and 5% for the 3-day ketoconazole, 1-day ketoconazole, and placebo groups, respectively (NNT = 1.5).
Prophylactic treatment for TV includes oral antifungal therapy with itraconazole 200 mg BID once a month for 6 months in patients who experience frequent disease recurrence.
Ketoconazole 400 mg once every month or 200 mg for 3 consecutive days every month is probably effective, but has not been studied in prospective RCTs.

Alternative treatment with a honey mixture containing honey, olive oil, and bees wax (1:1:1) applied three times daily for a maximum of 4 weeks has been shown to produce clinical and mycological cure.
Tinea versicolor (TV) is chronic (15%) and recurrent (50%) in some patients, necessitating retreatment, but it is generally a benign condition. C
TV is easily treatable; many effective treatments are available. B
Pigment changes may last for long periods of time even after an effective cure. C
TV is caused by a fungus that is normally present on the skin surface and therefore is not contagious.
Healing will continue after active treatment subsides and hypopigmentation may take weeks to months to resolve.
Disappearance of scales is the first sign of successful treatment.
Avoid applying oils to the skin.

Although tinea versicolor (TV) is most common between puberty and middle age when the sebaceous glands are most active, it has also been reported in the elderly over 60 years of age. One study found TV in 40.5% of the total 190 cases studied in this age group.
Wood's lamp exam in the elderly has a sensitivity of 38%.
TV has been reported in children and infants living in the tropics.
Face is more commonly involved in children.
Vinyl tape skin stripping may be preferred in children for sample collection. Using the side of a microscope slide also works and is safe.

Topical antifungals (eg, azole, allylamine, ciclopirox, or selenium sulfide).
If recurrent lesions, consider prophylactic oral antifungals (eg, itraconazole 200 mg orally twice a day 1 day per month).
Widespread lesions: consider oral antifungal (fluconazole, ketoconazole, or itraconazole).
Perform microscopic KOH using scalpel blade or vinyl tape sampling, or Wood's lamp fluorescence pale yellow to white.
Consider other diagnoses (eg, pityriasis rosea, vitiligo, tuberous sclerosis, seborrhea, secondary syphilis, leprosy).
